text: Snowflake has two types of users: PERSON and SERVICE. Which type is exempt from MFA enforcement?

options.A: PERSON users — they use SSO instead
options.B: SERVICE users (TYPE = SERVICE) — they are programmatic accounts exempt from MFA and must use key-pair or OAuth
options.D: Neither type — MFA is always optional

explanation: SERVICE users are created for programmatic (non-interactive) access and are exempt from MFA enforcement. They must authenticate using key-pair, OAuth, or similar non-password methods. PERSON users (human/interactive) are subject to MFA.

text: Future grants are configured for TABLES at both the database level (to ROLE_A) and the schema level (to ROLE_B) for the same schema. A new table is created. Which role receives the grant?

options.A: Both ROLE_A and ROLE_B receive the grant
options.B: Only ROLE_B — schema-level future grants take PRECEDENCE over database-level for the same object type
options.D: Neither — conflicting future grants cancel each other

explanation: When future grants for the same object type exist at both database and schema levels, schema-level grants take precedence and database-level grants are completely ignored for that object type in that schema.

text: An administrator wants to ensure that new tables created in a schema automatically receive SELECT grants for a specific role. Which feature accomplishes this?

options.A: Default privileges set at the account level
options.B: GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA to the role — future grants automatically apply to newly created objects
options.C: A stored procedure that runs after each CREATE TABLE
options.D: Tag-based automatic grants

explanation: Future grants (using ON FUTURE keyword) define an initial set of privileges automatically granted to a role when new objects of a specified type are created. This eliminates the need to manually grant after each object creation.

text: SECURITYADMIN has which global privilege that gives it authority to manage grants across the account?

options.B: MANAGE GRANTS — the global privilege to grant or revoke any privilege on any object
options.D: EXECUTE TASK

explanation: SECURITYADMIN holds the global MANAGE GRANTS privilege, allowing it to grant or revoke privileges on ANY object in the account, regardless of ownership. This is what makes it the access control authority.

text: An object owner grants SELECT on their table WITH GRANT OPTION to ROLE_A. What does WITH GRANT OPTION allow?

options.B: ROLE_A can further grant SELECT on that table to other roles
options.C: ROLE_A automatically gets all other privileges on the table
options.D: ROLE_A becomes the new owner

explanation: WITH GRANT OPTION allows the recipient role to further grant the same privilege to other roles. It does not confer ownership, other privileges, or DDL capabilities.

text: A network policy is set at the account level. Can it also be applied to a specific security integration (like SAML)?

options.A: No — network policies only apply at account or user level
options.B: Yes — network policies can be applied at the account level, user level, AND security integration level
options.D: Only at user level and integration level

explanation: Network policies can be applied at three levels: account level, user level, and security integration level. Integration-level policies control which IPs can use a specific authentication method (e.g., SAML SSO).

text: What happens when a user with no user-level network policy connects to an account that has NO account-level network policy?

options.B: Connection is ALLOWED from any IP — without a network policy, there is no IP restriction
options.D: A default policy restricting to RFC 1918 ranges applies

explanation: Without any network policy (account or user level), Snowflake allows connections from any IP address. Network policies are opt-in — they restrict access only when explicitly configured.

text: An authentication policy is created with MFA_ENROLLMENT = 'REQUIRED'. What does this enforce?

options.B: All human users in scope must enroll in MFA — they cannot authenticate without a second factor
options.D: MFA is enabled but can be bypassed with MINS_TO_BYPASS_MFA

explanation: MFA_ENROLLMENT = REQUIRED means all human users (TYPE = PERSON) covered by the policy MUST enroll in MFA. They will be prompted to set up a second factor on their next login. Service users are exempt.

text: MFA token caching allows users to avoid repeated MFA prompts. How long is a cached MFA token valid?

options.B: Up to 4 hours
options.D: Indefinitely until logout

explanation: A cached MFA token is valid for up to 4 hours. It is invalidated if: the ALLOW_CLIENT_MFA_CACHING parameter is set to FALSE, credentials change, or the token expires.

text: A user is locked out because they lost their MFA device. An admin needs to grant temporary access. What command allows bypassing MFA for a limited time?

options.B: ALTER USER ... SET MINS_TO_BYPASS_MFA = 30 — allows password-only login for 30 minutes
options.D: GRANT MFA_BYPASS TO USER

explanation: ALTER USER ... SET MINS_TO_BYPASS_MFA = N temporarily allows the user to authenticate with password only (no MFA) for N minutes. This is the emergency recovery mechanism for locked-out users.

text: Which TWO privileges are required for a role to USE a warehouse and query a table? (Select TWO)

options.B: USAGE on the warehouse
options.D: SELECT on the table (plus USAGE on database and schema)

explanation: To query: USAGE on warehouse (to submit queries), USAGE on database, USAGE on schema, and SELECT on table. OPERATE is for suspend/resume. MONITOR is for viewing activity. OWNERSHIP is full control.

text: The OWNERSHIP privilege on a table is transferred from ROLE_A to ROLE_B. What happens to existing SELECT grants on the table?

options.A: All existing grants are revoked when ownership transfers
options.B: Existing grants REMAIN intact — transferring OWNERSHIP does not revoke other privileges already granted
options.D: The table must be re-created under new ownership

explanation: Transferring OWNERSHIP changes who controls the object but does NOT revoke existing grants made by the previous owner. All previously granted privileges remain in effect unless explicitly revoked.

text: What is UBAC (User-Based Access Control) in Snowflake?

options.B: A complementary model that allows granting privileges DIRECTLY to individual users (not just roles) — useful for collaborative development scenarios
options.C: A legacy model that is deprecated
options.D: A mandatory security framework for all accounts

explanation: UBAC complements RBAC by allowing privileges to be granted directly to users (not through roles). It's intended for collaborative scenarios like Streamlit app development where granular per-user control is needed during development.

text: A projection policy is applied to a column. What does it control?

options.A: Whether the column value is masked
options.B: Which roles can include the column in a SELECT statement — unauthorized roles cannot project (select) the column at all
options.C: Whether the column can be used in a JOIN
options.D: The display format of the column

explanation: Projection policies control which roles can SELECT (project) a column. Unlike masking (which returns a transformed value), projection policies PREVENT the column from appearing in query output entirely for unauthorized roles.

text: An aggregation policy is applied to a table. What behavior does it enforce?

options.A: All queries must include a GROUP BY clause
options.B: Unauthorized roles must use aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG) — they cannot retrieve individual row-level data
options.C: The table can only store aggregated data
options.D: Only ACCOUNTADMIN can run analytics on the table

explanation: Aggregation policies require that unauthorized roles apply aggregate functions to protected columns. This prevents extracting individual records while still allowing statistical analysis (counts, sums, averages).

text: What is the difference between DIRECT_OBJECTS_ACCESSED and BASE_OBJECTS_ACCESSED in the ACCESS_HISTORY view?

options.A: They are identical — just different names
options.B: DIRECT = what the query SQL referenced (e.g., a view). BASE = the underlying objects the view reads from (e.g., tables).
options.C: DIRECT = tables only. BASE = views only.
options.D: DIRECT = current session. BASE = historical.

explanation: DIRECT_OBJECTS_ACCESSED: the object explicitly referenced in the SQL (could be a view). BASE_OBJECTS_ACCESSED: the underlying storage objects actually read (the tables behind the view). This enables complete lineage tracking.

text: SYSTEM$GET_TAG('pii_tag', 'my_db.my_schema.my_table.email', 'column') returns what?

options.A: The masking policy attached to the tag
options.B: The TAG VALUE assigned to that column for the specified tag — purely metadata retrieval
options.C: Whether the column is classified as PII
options.D: The column's data type

explanation: SYSTEM$GET_TAG retrieves the tag VALUE assigned to a specific object (table, column, schema, etc.) for a given tag name. It returns metadata only — it does not enforce anything.

text: A notification integration is configured for an alert. What delivery methods does it support?

options.B: Email and webhooks (Slack, PagerDuty, Microsoft Teams) via notification integrations
options.D: Snowsight dashboard notifications only

explanation: Notification integrations support email delivery and webhook delivery (Slack, PagerDuty, Teams, etc.). They are used by alerts, Snowpipe error notifications, and other event-driven features.

text: What categories does SYSTEM$CLASSIFY assign to detected sensitive columns?

options.B: Semantic categories (e.g., EMAIL, PHONE_NUMBER, NAME) and privacy categories (e.g., IDENTIFIER, QUASI_IDENTIFIER, SENSITIVE)
options.D: Encryption levels (HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW)

explanation: SYSTEM$CLASSIFY assigns both semantic categories (what type of data — email, SSN, phone) and privacy categories (how sensitive — IDENTIFIER, QUASI_IDENTIFIER, SENSITIVE). This dual classification guides masking decisions.

text: An object tagging policy propagates a tag from a TABLE to all columns within it. This is called what?

options.B: Tag lineage — tags propagate (inherit) from parent objects to child objects automatically
options.D: Tag replication

explanation: Tag lineage means tags applied to a parent (table, schema, database) propagate to child objects (columns, tables, schemas). This enables tag-based masking to protect many columns by tagging at a higher level.

text: A resource monitor has action DO SUSPEND vs DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE. What is the difference?

options.B: SUSPEND allows currently running queries to finish, then suspends. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE cancels all running queries and suspends instantly.
options.C: SUSPEND pauses for 5 minutes first. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE is instant.
options.D: SUSPEND only works at account level. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at warehouse level.

explanation: DO SUSPEND: graceful — running queries complete, then warehouse suspends. No new queries are accepted. DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE: forceful — all running queries are cancelled immediately, warehouse suspends instantly.

text: What is the NOTIFY action on a resource monitor trigger?

options.A: It suspends the warehouse and sends an email
options.B: It sends a notification to account administrators WITHOUT suspending the warehouse — queries continue running
options.C: It blocks new queries but lets existing ones finish
options.D: It reduces warehouse size automatically

explanation: DO NOTIFY sends an alert notification to account admins but takes NO action on the warehouse. Queries continue running. It's an early warning mechanism, typically set at lower thresholds (e.g., 75%) before suspend triggers.

text: Snowflake Budgets are used for cost control. How do they differ from resource monitors?

options.A: They are identical features with different names
options.B: Budgets can track SERVERLESS costs (Snowpipe, auto-clustering, etc.) while resource monitors only track user-managed warehouse credits
options.C: Resource monitors track more services than budgets
options.D: Budgets are only available on VPS edition

explanation: Budgets track serverless feature costs (Snowpipe, auto-clustering, MV maintenance, serverless tasks) that resource monitors cannot track. Resource monitors are limited to user-provisioned warehouse credits only.

text: LOGIN_HISTORY in ACCOUNT_USAGE records what information?

options.B: Authentication events including: user, timestamp, client IP, authentication method, success/failure status, and error details
options.D: Password change history

explanation: LOGIN_HISTORY records all authentication events — successful and failed — with details like user, IP, auth method (password, key-pair, SSO), success/failure, and error messages. Essential for security auditing.

text: What protocol does Snowflake use for federated single sign-on (SSO)?

options.B: SAML 2.0 — browser-based federated authentication with identity providers like Okta and Azure AD
options.D: Kerberos

explanation: Snowflake uses SAML 2.0 for federated SSO. It supports IdPs like Okta, Azure AD, ADFS, and others. SAML is browser-based — the user is redirected to the IdP for authentication, then back to Snowflake.

text: A key pair is rotated for a service account. The old public key is RSA_PUBLIC_KEY and the new one is set as RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2. Can both keys be active simultaneously?

options.A: No — only one key can be active at a time
options.B: Yes — Snowflake supports TWO active public keys simultaneously (RSA_PUBLIC_KEY and RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2) to enable zero-downtime key rotation
options.C: Yes, but only for 24 hours during transition
options.D: No — the old key is immediately revoked

explanation: Snowflake supports two simultaneous public keys (RSA_PUBLIC_KEY and RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2) per user. This enables zero-downtime rotation: set the new key as KEY_2, update clients, then remove the old key.

text: What is the PUBLIC role in Snowflake?

options.A: A role only ACCOUNTADMIN can use
options.B: A role that is automatically granted to EVERY user and role in the account — it serves as the baseline privilege set
options.C: An empty placeholder role with no purpose
options.D: The default role for new database objects

explanation: PUBLIC is automatically granted to every user and every role. It's the bottom of the role hierarchy — privileges granted to PUBLIC are available to everyone. Use it carefully; anything granted to PUBLIC is universally accessible.

text: What is the difference between Tri-Secret Secure and standard Snowflake encryption?

options.A: Standard uses no encryption; Tri-Secret adds AES-256
options.B: Standard uses Snowflake-managed AES-256. Tri-Secret adds a CUSTOMER-managed key — if the customer revokes their key, data becomes inaccessible even to Snowflake.
options.C: Tri-Secret uses three different encryption algorithms
options.D: Standard encrypts storage only; Tri-Secret adds transit encryption

explanation: Standard: Snowflake manages all encryption keys (AES-256 at rest, TLS in transit). Tri-Secret Secure: composite key = customer-managed key (in cloud KMS) + Snowflake key. Either party can revoke access independently.

text: Which TWO best practices does Snowflake recommend for the ACCOUNTADMIN role? (Select TWO)

options.A: Assign ACCOUNTADMIN to all users for convenience
options.B: Assign ACCOUNTADMIN to at least TWO users to avoid lockout scenarios
options.C: Require MFA for all ACCOUNTADMIN users
options.D: Use ACCOUNTADMIN as the default role for all sessions
options.E: Create all database objects with ACCOUNTADMIN

explanation: Best practices: (1) Assign ACCOUNTADMIN to at least 2 users (prevents single-point lockout — password reset takes up to 2 business days). (2) Require MFA for all ACCOUNTADMIN users. Do NOT use it as default role or for object creation.

text: Why does Snowflake recommend NOT using ACCOUNTADMIN to create database objects?

options.B: Objects owned by ACCOUNTADMIN require explicit grants to other roles — using SYSADMIN or lower roles integrates objects naturally into the role hierarchy
options.D: It's a legacy restriction with no technical reason

explanation: Objects created by ACCOUNTADMIN are isolated at the top of the hierarchy. Other roles can't access them without explicit grants. Using SYSADMIN (or subordinate roles) means the hierarchy naturally inherits access. Best practice: create with lower roles.

text: TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS in ACCOUNT_USAGE shows what storage breakdown for each table?

options.B: Active bytes, Time Travel bytes, AND Fail-safe bytes — the complete storage cost breakdown per table
options.D: Only compressed bytes

explanation: TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS provides per-table storage: ACTIVE_BYTES (current data), TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES (historical data retained), and FAILSAFE_BYTES (protection data). This helps identify tables with high protection overhead.

text: A masking policy uses IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('HR_ADMIN') instead of CURRENT_ROLE() = 'HR_ADMIN'. Why?

options.B: IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION checks ALL active roles (primary + secondary), while CURRENT_ROLE() only checks the primary role — preventing bypass when HR_ADMIN is a secondary role
options.D: IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION works in stored procedures; CURRENT_ROLE doesn't

explanation: CURRENT_ROLE() only returns the primary role. If HR_ADMIN is activated as a secondary role, CURRENT_ROLE() won't match. IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION checks the full role hierarchy graph, providing more reliable policy evaluation.

text: A stored procedure is created with EXECUTE AS CALLER. The caller has SELECT on table_a but the procedure owner does not. Can the procedure query table_a?

options.A: No — the procedure uses owner privileges
options.B: Yes — EXECUTE AS CALLER means the procedure runs with the CALLER's privileges, so if the caller has SELECT, it works
options.C: No — both caller and owner must have the privilege
options.D: Yes, but only if the caller is ACCOUNTADMIN

explanation: EXECUTE AS CALLER: procedure runs with the calling user's privileges. If the caller has SELECT on table_a, the procedure can access it regardless of the owner's privileges. This is useful for utilities that should respect caller permissions.

text: Can privileges be granted directly to a USER (not a role) in Snowflake?

options.A: No — all privileges must go through roles (RBAC only)
options.B: Yes — since UBAC (User-Based Access Control), privileges can be granted directly to users for collaborative scenarios
options.C: Only USAGE on warehouses can be granted to users directly
options.D: Only in VPS edition

explanation: With UBAC support, privileges can now be granted directly to individual users (not just roles). This complements RBAC for scenarios like Streamlit app development where per-user control during collaboration is needed.

text: A row access policy references a mapping table that lists which users can see which regions. The mapping table is dropped. What happens to queries on the protected table?

options.A: All rows are returned (policy becomes permissive)
options.B: ZERO rows are returned — the policy evaluation fails and defaults to denying all rows for safety
options.D: The policy is automatically disabled

explanation: If a row access policy references an object that is dropped or inaccessible, the policy evaluation fails/errors. In most configurations, this results in zero rows returned (deny-by-default). This is a safety mechanism — never silently grant access on failure.

text: GRANTS_TO_ROLES view in ACCOUNT_USAGE tracks what?

options.B: All privileges currently granted to roles in the account — a complete audit trail of who has access to what
options.D: Only future grants

explanation: GRANTS_TO_ROLES provides a comprehensive view of all privileges currently granted to all roles in the account. It includes object type, privilege, granted_to, grantee_name, and whether grant option is enabled.

text: An account is configured with SSO (SAML 2.0). Can users still log in with username/password if SSO is down?

options.A: No — once SSO is configured, password login is permanently disabled
options.B: Yes — unless an authentication policy explicitly restricts AUTHENTICATION_METHODS to only SAML, password login remains available as fallback
options.D: No — Snowflake requires SSO to be the only method

explanation: Configuring SSO does not automatically disable password login. Both methods coexist by default. Authentication policies can restrict which methods are allowed. 'Break glass' access typically preserves password + MFA for emergency admin access.

text: What does the OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES view in ACCOUNT_USAGE provide?

options.B: Object-to-object references — which views depend on which tables, which policies reference which columns, etc.
options.D: Compute dependencies between warehouses

explanation: OBJECT_DEPENDENCIES shows object-to-object references: views → tables, policies → columns, streams → tables, etc. This enables impact analysis before dropping or altering objects.

text: A resource monitor quota resets on what schedule?

options.B: Based on the FREQUENCY setting: DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY, YEARLY, or NEVER (quota applies once and doesn't reset)
options.D: Only when manually reset by ACCOUNTADMIN

explanation: Resource monitors have a configurable FREQUENCY: DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY, YEARLY, or NEVER. The quota resets at the start of each period. NEVER means the quota is a one-time lifetime limit.

text: What is the relationship between a security integration and SSO in Snowflake?

options.B: A security integration of TYPE = SAML2 defines the connection to an external IdP — it stores IdP metadata (SSO URL, certificate, issuer) for federated authentication
options.C: Security integrations only handle OAuth, not SAML
options.D: A security integration replaces network policies for SSO users

explanation: A security integration (TYPE = SAML2) configures the trust relationship between Snowflake and an external IdP. It stores the IdP's SSO URL, X.509 certificate, and issuer string. This is required for SAML-based federated login.
